children: By Steven Scheer

The Bank of Israel could continue reducing short-term interest rates should price pressures remain stable and depending on how the economy reacts to a third straight rate cut, deputy governor Andrew Abir said on Tuesday.

Abir told Reuters that a low inflation rate of 1.5% in July, which is below the midpoint of the government's annual 1%-3% target, was the main reason for the central bank's quarter-point cut that brought the benchmark interest rate (ILINR=ECI) to a nearly four-year low of 3.25%.
He noted that, helped by the shekel's strength against the dollar
, inflation in Israel was coming down in contrast to higher prices around the world.
"We didn't really see a compelling reason not to continue with the process of reducing interest rates," Abir said after Tuesday's rates decision.
Eight of 14 economists polled by Reuters had projected a pause in rate cuts.
ABIR SAYS GROWTH 'REASONABLE', NOT 'FANTASTIC'
Abir said that a 15.4% annualised gain in second-quarter economic growth was good but much of the gain was from production by Israeli companies abroad.

"Some people may have been looking at the headline GDP figure and thinking, 'All right, there's no real reason to cut'. But I think when you look a little bit deeper at the data, then the growth figures are reasonable, but they're not fantastic."
After three straight cuts and five since last November, future reductions remain dependent on upcoming data, Abir said.
The central bank's own economists currently forecast a rates floor of 3% by mid-2027. A new estimate will be published at the next decision on October 21.

"If inflation sort of stabilises and goes back up a bit, we could pause around these levels, or if it continues going down, or if there's a continued appreciation of the (shekel) currency, we could continue reducing rates," Abir said.

"It very much depends on the data that we see going forward, and ... we want to see how this third cut is absorbed by the economy, how the various agents react to it, how the foreign exchange market reacts to it. Obviously, we're still not in a world in which there is no geopolitical risk."
ELECTION DUE NEXT MONTH
Yet, Israel's risk premium and credit default swap rates are back to where they were before the start of the
in October 2023.
"We still live in a volatile part of the world, and that's certainly something that can change either way," Abir said.
The next rates decision comes just before Israel's national election on October 27. Abir said the vote played no part in the bank's decisions.
"We're driven by the data, not by the fact that there's an election coming up at the end of October," he said.
"For us, the key thing is definitely inflation data — do we need to run interest rates that are 3-1/2% to keep inflation at the middle of our range? No."
